definition.text: The exchange of capital, goods and services across national borders to meet a need or demand.

facts.text: A product sold from one country to another is an export for the seller's country and an import for the buyer's.
It is usually more costly than domestic trade because of tariffs and non-tariff barriers such as border delays, language and legal differences.
Because capital and labour move less easily between countries, a country can instead import goods that embody those inputs.
In 2025 world trade totalled 80,733 billion US dollars, of which merchandise made up 52,865 billion.
Mineral fuels and oils were the top traded commodity by export value in 2022.
Organisations such as the World Trade Organization work to ease and expand trade between countries.
A 2020 study of 189 countries found most are more exposed to over-exploited water, energy and land resources through trade, mainly from distant sources.

title: Trade versus local production
article: International trade#International trade vs local production

definition.text: The debate over whether goods, especially food, should be produced locally or imported, weighing environmental, economic and security effects.

facts.text: Studies find food miles are a relatively minor source of carbon emissions, though localising food may allow recycling of energy, water and nutrients.
Different harvest seasons can make importing from far away greener than local storage or greenhouse growing.
A 2020 study found local crops within 100 km could not meet demand for most food crops for 72-89% of the world's population.
Studies disagree on jobs: one found trade can raise local employment, another that import exposure cut local employment and labour income.
Regional differences can make some places better suited to a product, favouring trade; local production may need policies such as eco-tariffs to compete.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on the environmental and employment trade-offs between local and distant production.

title: Non-tariff barriers to trade

definition.text: Restrictions on imports or exports other than tariffs, such as quotas, licences, subsidies, customs delays and technical standards.

facts.text: They are controversial because they may comply with trade rules yet serve protectionist purposes.
A 2019 UNCTAD report found trade costs from non-tariff measures were more than double those of traditional tariffs.
As tariffs fell through GATT and WTO negotiation rounds, protectionism turned to new measures such as technical barriers to trade.
They are grouped as protectionist, assistance (such as domestic subsidies) or non-protectionist, the last aimed at health, safety and the environment.
Most can be called protectionist unless they address market problems such as externalities or information asymmetries, as safety standards and labels do.
Rising consumer demand for safe and environmentally friendly products has made technical barriers to trade more popular.

contested_note: Whether particular non-tariff measures protect health and environment or disguise protectionism is disputed.

definition.text: Product standards on labelling, testing and composition that protect health and the environment but can also keep out foreign goods.

facts.text: Standards enacted for health and safety can be used for protectionist and political ends.
Tariffs raise marginal costs and grow with volume, while testing or labelling rules impose fixed costs.
Fixed compliance costs can push small exporters out while leaving large multinationals untouched, shifting profits toward them.
This logic explains why large chemical producers supported the EU's REACH regulation.
Non-protectionist barriers include import bans based on objectionable harvesting or fishing methods.

definition.text: A limit, by value or quantity, on how much of a good may be imported or exported over a period.

facts.text: Quotas usually raise costs, narrow consumers' choice and raise import prices for companies.
'Voluntary' export restraints are limits an exporter accepts under threat of sanctions.
Embargoes are the extreme case: an outright ban on trade in certain goods.

title: Pollution haven hypothesis

definition.text: The idea that firms investing abroad move to countries with cheap resources and weak environmental rules, making those countries havens for pollution.

facts.text: Countries with stricter environmental rules become more expensive for firms because of compliance costs.
Regulations raise input costs for pollution-intensive goods and reduce a place's comparative advantage, pushing firms to lower-standard countries.
Evidence supports the weaker claims that pollution control costs affect trade and investment, but their importance relative to other factors is still controversial.
After the US tightened lead air standards in 2009, exports of used lead-acid batteries to Mexico rose four-fold, followed by more low-birth-weight babies near Mexican recycling plants.
It may partly explain the environmental Kuznets curve, as polluting industry shifts from richer to poorer economies.
It has three strengths: pollution costs matter at the margin; they measurably shift trade and investment; or countries deliberately set standards too low to attract investment.
The first two versions have empirical support, but how much the effect matters next to other trade and investment factors is disputed.
Economists model economic activity as falling with regulatory stringency, because regulation raises input costs and erodes comparative advantage in pollution-intensive goods.

contested_note: How much environmental rules actually drive firm location, compared with other factors, remains disputed.

definition.text: The intergovernmental organization, formed in 1995, that regulates and eases trade between countries.

facts.text: Its forerunner, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), was set up by 23 countries in 1947; its early negotiating rounds concentrated on cutting tariffs.
The Marrakesh Agreement, signed on 15 April 1994 at the end of the Uruguay Round, officially established the WTO.
It has 166 members and 23 observer governments.
It provides a forum for negotiations and settling disputes, reviews national trade policies and helps poorer countries adjust to its rules.
It sets the rules of trade policy rather than outcomes, and members agree to settle disputes through it rather than act alone.
Studies find it boosted trade; without it, the average country would face tariffs on its exports 32 percentage points higher.
The Doha Round, launched in 2001 to make globalization help the world's poor, stalled over farm subsidies, industrial tariffs and non-tariff barriers.
Its director-general has called for reform of subsidy and competition rules, decision-making and global public goods such as climate protection.

title: Environmental exceptions in trade rules
article: World Trade Organization#Principles of the trading system

definition.text: Provisions in WTO agreements that let countries restrict trade to protect the environment and health, as long as the measures are not disguised protectionism.

facts.text: In specific circumstances governments may restrict trade: WTO agreements allow measures to protect the environment as well as public, animal and plant health.
Members must not use environmental protection measures as a way of disguising protectionist policies.
The WTO's Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures governs quarantine rules for pests and diseases.
In 2006 the WTO ruled that the European Union broke trade law between 1999 and 2003 with its moratorium on approving imports of genetically modified organisms.
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety states that trade and environment agreements should be mutually supportive.
In 2024 US Democrats argued that a carbon border adjustment is a fee permissible under WTO rules, not a carbon tax.

title: Most-favoured-nation and national treatment
article: World Trade Organization#Principles of the trading system

definition.text: The WTO's non-discrimination rule: a member must offer all other members equal terms and treat imports no worse than its own goods.

facts.text: Most-favoured-nation treatment means the best terms a member gives any WTO member for a product must be given to all members.
Exceptions include free trade agreements and preferential treatment for developing countries.
National treatment means imports must be treated no less favourably than domestic goods once inside the market; it targets non-tariff barriers such as discriminatory technical standards.
The WTO's other key principles are reciprocity, binding and enforceable commitments, transparency and safety valves.

title: Criticism of the WTO

definition.text: Arguments that WTO-led trade liberalisation has not delivered the promised growth, poverty reduction and fair sharing of gains.

facts.text: Ha-Joon Chang notes that developing countries grew faster in 1960–1980 than in 1980–2000, even though their trade policies are now far more liberal.
Critics say the benefits of WTO-backed free trade are not shared equally, pointing to widening gaps between rich and poor.
Liberalising too early is feared to trap developing economies in the primary sector, which often needs little skilled labour.
Vietnam cut poverty and grew fast while liberalising slowly with safeguards, whereas El Salvador's growth stayed weak after it removed import barriers and cut tariffs.

contested_note: Studies credit the WTO with boosting trade, while critics dispute that liberalisation reliably brings growth and less poverty.

title: Global waste trade

definition.text: The international trade in waste, shipped between countries for treatment, disposal or recycling.

facts.text: Toxic or hazardous wastes are often imported by developing countries from developed ones.
Richer, more urbanised countries produce more solid waste, and waste mostly flows from the Global North to be disposed of in the Global South.
Scholars link its sharp growth to the free-market policies of the 1980s, which pushed developing countries to import waste as a route to economic expansion.
Supporters argue that importing waste can stimulate the economies of countries with little else to offer the global economy.
Critics note that most hazardous waste is produced in the United States and Europe, yet the health harms fall on poorer countries that did not produce it.
Poorer countries often lack safe recycling facilities, so people handle toxic waste by hand and poor disposal poisons the surroundings, causing illness and death.
Areas around dump sites carry very high levels of heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants that kill birds, fish and other wildlife.
It is hard to regulate: volumes are huge, laws are hard to enforce, and vague definitions let hazardous waste be exported as commodities or raw materials.

related: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South
contested_note: Supporters see waste imports as an economic opportunity for poor countries, while critics see them as dumping that harms health and deepens inequality.

title: Economic case for the waste trade

definition.text: The argument that sending hazardous waste to low-wage, less polluted countries makes economic sense, famously made in a 1991 memo by Lawrence Summers.

facts.text: Summers, then World Bank chief economist, wrote that the economic logic of dumping toxic waste in the lowest-wage country was 'impeccable'.
The memo called countries in Africa 'vastly under polluted' and asked whether the World Bank should encourage dirty industries to move to the least developed countries.
A Cato Institute article argued that people in developing countries would rationally accept more exposure to pollutants in exchange for higher productivity and income.
The case rests mainly on the view that developing countries need to further their economic development.

contested_note: Supporters call waste imports rational development; critics call the practice toxic colonialism.

title: Toxic colonialism

definition.text: The use of poorer countries as cheap places to export or dump the hazardous waste of developed countries.

facts.text: It is the core critique of the global waste trade.
The term uses 'colonialism' because economic dependence, exploitation of labour and cultural inequality mark both.
T.V. Reed links it to colonial views of indigenous land as empty 'waste', which make Global South land seem expendable for Western wastes.
Laura Pratt argues international agreements have not stopped it, because waste moves under false permits, bribes, improper labels or the pretext of recycling.

related: Hazardous waste exports to the Global South
Economic case for the waste trade

definition.text: The shipment of discarded electrical and electronic devices, mostly from rich countries, to developing countries for processing and recycling.

facts.text: An estimated 50 million tons of e-waste are produced each year, mostly in the United States and Europe, and most is shipped to Asia and Africa.
Its growth comes from fast technological change, falling prices and planned obsolescence.
Heavy metals and toxins leak into waterways and groundwater, exposing dump workers, children searching for items to sell and nearby residents.
Guiyu, China, possibly the world's largest e-waste dump, has workers dismantling over 1.5 million pounds of junked electronics a year.

definition.text: Dismantling old ships, which industrialised countries increasingly send to Asia because it is cheaper there.

facts.text: China and Bangladesh are the two hubs of shipbreaking in Asia.
Old ships were built under weaker environmental rules and contain asbestos, lead oxide, mercury, arsenic and tributyltin.
Workers traditionally lack proper equipment or protective gear when handling these substances.

definition.text: The international trade in waste plastics, identified as the main cause of marine litter.

facts.text: Countries importing waste plastics often lack the capacity to process all of it.
The United Nations therefore restricts trade in plastic waste unless it meets certain criteria.
In 2018 Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte threatened war unless Canada took back 64 tonnes of garbage, shipped by a plastic-recycling firm and mislabelled as recyclable.

definition.text: A 1991 treaty in which African nations, unhappy with the Basel Convention, banned imports of hazardous waste.

facts.text: Unlike the Basel Convention, it bans imports of all hazardous waste generated outside the Organization of African Unity and treats imports from non-parties as illegal.
Limited resources and weak enforcement meant members could not stop toxic dumping, so its application was very limited.
Similarly, the Lomé IV Convention banned exports of hazardous wastes from the European Community to African, Caribbean and Pacific states.

definition.text: A duty imposed by a national government or union on imported goods, paid by the importer.

facts.text: Besides raising revenue, import duties regulate foreign trade by burdening foreign products to encourage or safeguard domestic industry.
Protective tariffs are among the most widely used tools of protectionism, along with import and export quotas and other non-tariff barriers.

Economic analyses generally find tariffs distort the free market and raise prices of both foreign and domestic products; welfare effects on the importing country are usually negative even without retaliation.
Douglas Irwin says tariffs have served three purposes: revenue, protection of domestic producers, and securing reciprocity through trade agreements.
From 1790 to 1860 US import duties made up about 90% of federal receipts; the 1930 Smoot-Hawley act raised the average tariff on dutiable imports from about 40% to 47%.
Duty is often charged ad valorem on a transaction value, with goods identified by Harmonized System codes developed by the World Customs Organization.

definition.text: A tariff set to maximise the welfare of the country imposing it.

facts.text: Free trade is often the best policy for efficiency, but levying a tariff is sometimes second best.

title: Infant industry argument
article: Tariff#Arguments used by proponents of tariffs > Infant industry argument

definition.text: The claim that emerging industries, especially in less-developed countries, need temporary protection from established foreign competitors.

facts.text: Mainstream economists accept tariffs can help industries develop in the short term, but this depends on the protection being temporary and on the government's ability to manage it.
Most economists, following comparative advantage, argue struggling industries should not be maintained by protection.

contested_note: Protectionists argue for temporary protection while most economists doubt it works.

title: Environmental dumping argument
article: Tariff#Arguments used by proponents of tariffs > Protection against environmental dumping

definition.text: The argument for tariffs where firms gain unfair competition from weaker environmental regulation elsewhere.

facts.text: The EU starts its carbon border-adjustment mechanism in 2026 to level the playing field with firms not subject to European carbon pricing.

definition.text: A controlling ownership stake in a company or asset in one country held by an investor, firm or government from another country.

facts.text: Control distinguishes it from foreign portfolio investment, a passive holding of foreign stocks and bonds.
The World Bank's narrow definition is a lasting management interest of 10% or more of voting stock in an enterprise abroad.
Broadly it covers mergers and acquisitions, new facilities, reinvested profits and intracompany loans, and usually involves management participation and transfer of technology and expertise.
Before Stephen Hymer's 1960 work no theory dealt specifically with FDI; Heckscher and Ohlin's factor-proportions logic had treated foreign investment generally.
A 2010 meta-analysis found foreign investment robustly raises local firms' productivity growth in developing and transition countries.
Incentives to attract FDI include low corporate and income tax rates and exemptions from regulations, usually for very large projects.

definition.text: FDI is classified from the investor's view as horizontal, vertical or conglomerate, and from the host country's view by its purpose.

facts.text: Horizontal FDI duplicates a multinational's home industry chain in the destination country to make similar goods.
Vertical FDI buys a firm to exploit natural resources in the host country (backward) or distribution outlets to market its products there (forward).
Conglomerate FDI combines horizontal and vertical; platform FDI invests in one country to export to a third.
Host-country classes are import-substituting, export-increasing and government-initiated FDI.
